content: 1. Kissinger et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness of patient-delivered partner treatment for Trichomonas vaginalis infections. The study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2006. 2. Schwebke and Desmond performed a randomized controlled trial to compare different partner notification methods aimed at preventing trichomoniasis in women. Their findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 3. Cleveland conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of alternative methods for gonorrhea contact referral and rescreening in Dade County, as reported by the Dade County Department of Public Health in 1994. 4. Potterat and Rothenberg presented a preliminary report on the case-finding effectiveness of self-referral systems for gonorrhea in the American Journal of Public Health. 5. Solomon and DeJong investigated the impact of an educational videotape shown in clinics on the knowledge and treatment behaviors of men diagnosed with gonorrhea. Their study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 6. Kerani et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial to assess the use of inSPOT and patient-delivered partner therapy for gonorrhea and chlamydial infections among men who have sex with men. The results were published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 7. Kissinger et al. evaluated patient-delivered partner treatment for male urethritis in a randomized controlled trial, with findings published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2005. 8. Wilson et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial to reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections through enhanced patient-based partner notification. The study was published in the American Journal of Public Health. 9. Andersen et al. compared home sampling with conventional contact tracing for detecting Chlamydia trachomatis infections in male partners of infected women. Their randomized study was published in BMJ. 10. Apoola and Beardsley examined whether adding a urine testing kit to contact slips increased partner notification rates for genital chlamydial infections. Their findings were published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS. 11. Cameron et al. tested novel interventions to reduce reinfection rates in women with chlamydia through a randomized controlled trial, as reported in Human Reproduction. 12. Falk et al. explored the use of home sampling as a tool for partner notification in Chlamydia trachomatis infections through a randomized controlled trial published in Acta Dermato-Venereologica. 13. Low et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate partner notification for chlamydia infections in primary care settings, analyzing resource use. The study was published in BMJ in 2006. 14. Tomnay et al. investigated whether the internet could assist clients in conducting contact tracing through a randomized controlled trial using web-based information. The study was published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS. 15. Clark et al. piloted a randomized controlled trial in Lima, Peru, to assess the use of traditional and web-based technologies for improving partner notification following syphilis diagnosis among men who have sex with men. The findings were published in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. 16. Katz et al. evaluated the efficiency and cost-effectiveness of field follow-up for patients with Chlamydia trachomatis infections in a sexually transmitted diseases clinic. The study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 1988. 17. Trent et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial to assess the impact of a brief behavioral intervention for pelvic inflammatory disease in adolescents. The results were published in the Journal of Pediatric and Adolescent Gynecology. 18. Moyo et al. studied the impact of a single counseling session on partner referral for sexually transmitted disease treatment in Harare, Zimbabwe. The findings were published in AIDS and Behavior. 19. Faxelid et al. explored the role of individual counseling in improving partner notification for sexually transmitted diseases in Zambia. The study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 20. Nuwaha et al. assessed the efficacy of patient-delivered partner medication for treating sexual partners in Uganda. The study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 21. Brown et al. demonstrated that HIV partner notification is both effective and feasible in sub-Saharan Africa, highlighting opportunities for HIV treatment and prevention. The study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 22. Landis et al. reported the results of a randomized trial on partner notification for HIV cases in North Carolina, published in the New England Journal of Medicine. 23. Rosenberg et al. conducted an unblinded randomized controlled trial in Malawi to recruit male partners for couple HIV testing and counseling as part of the Option B+ program. The study was published in The Lancet HIV. 24. Cherutich et al. evaluated assisted partner services for HIV in Kenya through a cluster randomized controlled trial, with findings published in The Lancet HIV. 25. Schillinger et al. investigated the use of azithromycin in patient-delivered partner treatment to prevent repeated Chlamydia trachomatis infections among women. The study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 26. Golden et al. assessed the uptake and population-level impact of expedited partner therapy (EPT) for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in Washington State through a community-level randomized trial. The findings were published in PLOS Medicine. 27. Golden et al. also evaluated the effect of expedited treatment of sex partners on recurrent or persistent gonorrhea or chlamydial infections, as reported in the New England Journal of Medicine. 28. Gift et al. analyzed the cost and cost-effectiveness of expedited partner therapy compared to standard partner referral for treating chlamydia or gonorrhea. The study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 29. Silva-Santisteban et al. conducted a randomized community-level combination HIV prevention intervention for men who have sex with men in Peru, as reported in Sexually Transmitted Infections. 30. Balfour et al. explored young women's decisions to accept chlamydia screening, focusing on the influence of stigma and doctor-patient interactions. The study was published in BMC Public Health.
